hints: Look at the last pile. You either take it or you don't. What does each choice mean for the pile right before it?
Linear recursion turned into DP: best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + coins[i]). Keep only the two previous best totals.

1. Keep skip = 0 (best total up to pile i-2) and take = 0 (best total up to pile i-1).
  2. For each pile value v: cur = max(take, skip + v).
  3. Shift: skip = take, take = cur.
  4. Return take.

approaches.name: Try all subsets
approaches.idea: Pick or skip each pile recursively, rejecting choices with two neighbours taken.

approaches.name: Optimal: two running values
approaches.idea: Only the previous two best totals are needed.

explain: For [4,1,2,7,5,3,1] the best totals by prefix are 4, 4, 6, 11, 11, 14, 14. At pile 7 we compare skipping it (4) with taking it plus the best up to two piles back (4+7 = 11). The answer is 14 (4 + 7 + 3). The invariant is that after each pile, take is the best total using only piles up to it. A single pile just returns its value.
recognize: Pick items from a line to maximise a total, with a rule that no two neighbours can both be picked → take/skip recursion on the prefix.
javascript: function rob(coins) { let a = 0, b = 0; for (const c of coins) { const nb = Math.max(b, a + c); a = b; b = nb; } return b; }
